node.title: Mitochondrial cristae surface area
node.canonical_question: Why do mitochondria have inner membrane folds called cristae?
node.summary: Cristae dramatically increase inner membrane surface area. More surface means more ATP synthase complexes and higher ATP output.

seeds.title: Cristae function in energy output
seeds.canonical_question: What is the function of cristae in the inner mitochondrial membrane?

parsed.rendering_md:
## Why do mitochondrial inner membrane folds matter for energy production?

The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is not flat — it is folded into finger-like projections called **cristae**. These folds are not just a structural quirk; they have a direct impact on how much ATP a cell can make.

**Surface area is the key idea.** ATP synthase is a protein embedded in the inner membrane. The more inner membrane there is, the more copies of ATP synthase can fit. More ATP synthase molecules working at once means the cell can produce ATP at a higher rate.

Think of it like this: if you want to pack as many solar panels as possible onto a roof, you get more power if the roof has ridges and folds rather than being completely flat. Cristae do the same job — they multiply the effective area available for energy-producing machinery inside the mitochondrion.

The proton gradient (the build-up of protons in the space between the two membranes) also benefits from a larger inner membrane area, because there is more surface across which protons can be pumped by the electron transport chain complexes.

**In short:** cristae increase inner membrane surface area → more ATP synthase complexes → higher ATP output for the cell.
